metadata.title: Legumes - Nitrogen Fixation and Protein Architecture

sections.text: Legumes (family Fabaceae) are the second most important crop family after grasses. They are the primary protein source for most of the world's population, and uniquely, they can fix atmospheric nitrogen — effectively making their own fertilizer and enriching soil for subsequent crops.

metadata.title: Legumes - Nitrogen Fixation and Protein Architecture

sections.text:

  │   └── Mung bean / adzuki (Vigna): East/South Asia; sprouts, red bean paste
  │
  ├── CICEREAE tribe
  │   └── Chickpea (Cicer arietinum): Fertile Crescent; desi (small, colored) / kabuli (large, beige)

sections.text: ## Nitrogen Fixation: The Chemistry

metadata.title: Legumes - Nitrogen Fixation and Protein Architecture

sections.text: This is the most important biochemical pathway in agriculture. Most crop plants cannot access atmospheric N₂ directly. Legumes have a bacterial partner that does.

metadata.title: Legumes - Nitrogen Fixation and Protein Architecture

sections.text: ### The Chemistry

metadata.title: Legumes - Nitrogen Fixation and Protein Architecture

sections.text:
```
LEGUME ROOT NODULE FORMATION
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Legume root exudes flavonoids (signal molecules)
       │
       ▼
2. Rhizobium bacteria respond → produce Nod factors (lipochitooligosaccharides)
       │
       ▼
3. Root hair curls around bacteria → infection thread forms
       │
       ▼
4. Bacteria enter root cortex cells → multiply
       │
       ▼
5. Bacteria differentiate into BACTEROIDS (nitrogen-fixing form)
       │
       ▼
6. NODULE forms: specialized organ, pink/red when active
       │
       ▼
7. Plant provides: photosynthate (sucrose) for bacterial energy
   Bacteria provide: NH₃ for plant protein synthesis

metadata.title: Legumes - Nitrogen Fixation and Protein Architecture

sections.text:
LEGHEMOGLOBIN: pink/red color of active nodule
  - Plant-derived globin protein + iron-heme cofactor
  - Binds O₂ with high affinity (similar to hemoglobin)
  - Maintains very low [O₂] around bacteroids while allowing respiration
  - Without it: nitrogenase destroyed, no N₂ fixation
  - Globin proteins are ancient and widespread; leghemoglobin is a plant-bacterial
    symbiosis adaptation, not an animal-gene import.
```

sections.text: **Comparison:** Synthetic fertilizer (Haber-Bosch process, natural gas → NH₃) costs ~$500/tonne N. Biological fixation = free, but requires legume rotation.

sections.text:
MENDEL'S EXPERIMENTS (1856–1863):
  Gregor Mendel chose pea because:
    → Short generation time (3-4 months)
    → Self-pollinating by default (true-breeding lines easily maintained)
    → Distinct, clearly separable traits (seed color, seed shape, pod color, etc.)
    → Easily cross-pollinated manually (remove anthers, apply foreign pollen)
  Seven traits studied → discovered particulate inheritance (genes, called "factors")
  Results published 1866 → ignored until rediscovered 1900 by de Vries, Correns, von Tschermak
  Mendel's peas established the particulate theory of inheritance (chromosome theory came later, Sutton & Boveri c. 1902)

sections.text: **Not all legumes fix nitrogen.** The Rhizobium symbiosis is not universal within Fabaceae. Some species fix little. And even nitrogen-fixing legumes require the right Rhizobium strain — inoculation with the correct strain is commercially sold for farmers.

sections.text: ## The Big Picture

metadata.title: Root Crops and Tubers - Underground Storage, Global Consequences

sections.text: Root crops and tubers are concentrated carbohydrate storage organs. They were humanity's caloric insurance policy — underground, frost-protected, harvestable on demand, dramatically more calories per acre than grain in many conditions. The potato alone may have changed European history more than any political revolution.

metadata.title: Root Crops and Tubers - Underground Storage, Global Consequences

sections.text:
```
ROOT/TUBER CROP COMPARISON
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Crop         Origin           Calorie yield    Key advantage
             (region)         (kcal/ha/day)
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Potato       Andes            ~8,000-10,000    Temperate, calorie-dense
Sweet potato Andes            ~6,000-8,000     Tropical/subtropical, fast
Cassava      S. America       ~5,000-7,000     Most drought-tolerant food crop
Yam          Africa/Asia      ~2,000-4,000     Tropical, long storage life
Wheat        Fertile Crescent ~2,000-4,000     Comparison reference
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tuber crops generally provide more calories/acre in wet climates than grains.
The trade-off: lower protein content, higher water content, less storage life.
```

sections.text: **Chuño**: Andean freeze-dried potato, technology dating to ~1000 CE or earlier. Freeze overnight at altitude, stomp out water, freeze again, sun-dry. Result: 10-year shelf-stable lightweight food. Inca military logistics depended on it. The engineering is essentially the same as modern freeze-drying.

sections.text: ### The Irish Famine (1845-1852)

metadata.title: Root Crops and Tubers - Underground Storage, Global Consequences

sections.text: The catastrophic result of over-reliance on one potato variety.

metadata.title: Root Crops and Tubers - Underground Storage, Global Consequences

sections.text:
```
STRUCTURAL VULNERABILITY
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Ireland's political economy by 1845:
  Landlord class (mostly English Protestant) owned all land
  Catholic tenant farmers: subsistence on potato (Lumper variety)
  ~40% of population ate NOTHING BUT potatoes + milk
  Lumper: high yield, but genetically uniform (clonally propagated)
         virtually NO disease resistance

sections.text:
POLITICAL DIMENSION:
  British government's laissez-faire response (continued grain exports from
  Ireland during famine; "let the market work") is historically contested

sections.text: ## Sweet Potato (*Ipomoea batatas*): The Polynesian Mystery

metadata.title: Root Crops and Tubers - Underground Storage, Global Consequences

sections.text:
ANOMALY:
  Polynesia (Cook Islands, Marquesas) had sweet potato BEFORE Columbus
  Radiocarbon dates: Cook Islands sweet potato ~1000-1100 CE
  Name: "kumara" (Polynesian) ≈ "cumar" (Quechua, Peruvian language)
  Linguistic evidence: same root word across Pacific

HOW?
  Option A: Polynesians reached South America and brought sweet potato back
            Evidence: Polynesian DNA in some indigenous South American groups
            (Thor Heyerdahl's "Kon-Tiki" theory, now partially vindicated by genetics)
  Option B: South Americans reached Polynesia

  Genetic and linguistic evidence supports pre-Columbian contact between
  Polynesians and South Americans, likely around the late first or early second
  millennium CE, but the exact direction and number of transfers remain debated.
```

sections.text: ## Cassava (*Manihot esculenta*): The Cyanide Detox Crop

metadata.title: Root Crops and Tubers - Underground Storage, Global Consequences

sections.text: ### The Cyanide Problem

metadata.title: Root Crops and Tubers - Underground Storage, Global Consequences

sections.text:
TWO FORMS:
  "Sweet" cassava:  <100 mg HCN per kg fresh weight
                    Can be peeled, boiled, eaten
  "Bitter" cassava: 100-500 mg HCN per kg

metadata.title: Root Crops and Tubers - Underground Storage, Global Consequences

sections.text:
Cassava grows where wheat, rice, and potato fail:
- Survives prolonged drought (starch remains in roots even when leaves die)
- Grows in poor, acidic, low-nutrient soils
- No pre-prepared seedbed required
- Tubers stay in ground for 1-3 years (living storage = on-demand food)
- Highest calorie yield per hectare of any crop in tropical dry conditions

metadata.title: Root Crops and Tubers - Underground Storage, Global Consequences

sections.text: This is why cassava is the caloric staple for ~750 million people, primarily in sub-Saharan Africa and tropical South America.

|----------------------------|------------|------------|
| Potato population effect | Calories per acre plus small-plot subsistence | Demography also depends on land tenure, milk, and political economy |
| Irish Famine causation | *Phytophthora infestans*, Lumper monoculture, colonial policy | Not a purely natural disaster |

| Why cassava persists | Drought tolerance, poor-soil performance, living storage | Low protein and processing burden are the tradeoffs |

metadata.title: Root Crops and Tubers - Underground Storage, Global Consequences

sections.text: **Sweet potato ≠ yam.** Two different plant families. In US grocery stores, the soft orange variety (often called "yam") is a sweet potato (*Ipomoea batatas*). True yams (*Dioscorea*) are rarely found in US stores; common in West African and Caribbean markets.

metadata.title: Root Crops and Tubers - Underground Storage, Global Consequences

sections.text: **Cassava ≠ always dangerous.** Proper preparation (peeling, soaking, fermenting, cooking) makes cassava safe. Billions eat it daily. The danger is specifically from bitter cassava improperly processed, usually in conflict/famine conditions.

metadata.title: Root Crops and Tubers - Underground Storage, Global Consequences

sections.text: **The Irish Famine was not inevitable.** Ireland was exporting grain during the famine. Other crops were not failing — only potato. Whether this represents criminal negligence, deliberate policy, or laissez-faire ideology depends on historiographical position, but the famine was not purely a natural disaster.

metadata.title: Root Crops and Tubers - Underground Storage, Global Consequences

sections.text: **Potato wasn't immediately accepted in Europe.** In France, Antoine-Augustin Parmentier had to lobby extensively (and trick people) to get potato adopted ~1770s. In Prussia, Frederick the Great issued royal decrees. "Toxic nightshade relative" stigma + peasant conservatism were real barriers.

metadata.title: Fruits - Apple, Citrus, Banana, and the Geometry of Seed Dispersal

sections.text: Botanically, a fruit is any seed-bearing structure derived from the ovary of a flowering plant. This includes tomatoes, cucumbers, squash, and peppers — culinary "vegetables" that are botanically fruits. The evolutionary purpose is seed dispersal: fruits attract animals that consume the flesh and disperse seeds.

metadata.title: Fruits - Apple, Citrus, Banana, and the Geometry of Seed Dispersal

sections.text:
KEY PROPAGATION PATTERNS:
  Grafting/budding: prevents genetic variation in seeds; maintains cultivar;
    standard for tree fruits (apple scions on rootstock = clonal flavor consistency)
  Vegetative (runners, corms, offsets): inherently clonal; fast; banana model
  Seed: genetic recombination; used for annual crops, papaya; loses cultivar fidelity

metadata.title: Fruits - Apple, Citrus, Banana, and the Geometry of Seed Dispersal

sections.text:
FRUIT TYPES — BOTANICAL CLASSIFICATION
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SIMPLE FRUITS (from single flower, single ovary)

sections.text: The category "vegetable" is culinary, not botanical — it includes leaves, stems, roots, flowers, seeds, and fruits from dozens of unrelated plant families. This is an agricultural system design problem, not a fixed biological necessity.

sections.text: ## The Big Picture

metadata.title: Sugar Crops - Sugarcane, Sugar Beet, and the Sweetness Economy

sections.text: Sugar went from luxury to commodity to ubiquitous food additive in 400 years. In 1700, European per-capita sugar consumption was ~2 kg/year (expensive luxury). By 2000, it was ~40 kg/year. This transformation required: (1) Caribbean plantation slavery, (2) sugar beet to break the monopoly, and (3) high-fructose corn syrup to make sweetness cheap at industrial scale. Each step reshaped geopolitics.

sections.text: ## Sugar and Slavery: The Nexus

metadata.title: Sugar Crops - Sugarcane, Sugar Beet, and the Sweetness Economy

sections.text: The Caribbean plantation system was the most profitable economic enterprise of the 17th-18th centuries. It was entirely dependent on enslaved labor.

metadata.title: Sugar Crops - Sugarcane, Sugar Beet, and the Sweetness Economy

sections.text:
```
THE PLANTATION ECONOMY
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
WHY SUGAR REQUIRED ENSLAVED LABOR:
  Sugarcane harvest: intensely physical, hot, dangerous
  Processing: 24/7 (sugar juice must be processed immediately)
  Mill work: dangerous machinery (limb loss common)
  Scale required: economically viable only at large scale
  Cost: European contract labor was too expensive and too unwilling

metadata.title: Sugar Crops - Sugarcane, Sugar Beet, and the Sweetness Economy

sections.text:
SCALE OF THE TRADE:
  1501-1866: ~12.5 million Africans shipped
  ~2 million died during Middle Passage (15-20% mortality)
  Destinations: Brazil (~45%), Caribbean (~40%), US (~5%), elsewhere
  Barbados, Jamaica, Saint-Domingue (Haiti): pure sugar economies
  Saint-Domingue (Haiti) by 1789: most profitable colony in the world
    Produced 40% of Europe's sugar + 60% of coffee
    On 680 sq miles, worked by ~480,000 enslaved people

sections.text:
THE HAITIAN REVOLUTION (1791-1804):
  Only successful slave revolution in history
  Enslaved Haitians overthrew French colonialism
  Result: Haiti independent 1804; French colony destroyed
  France demanded 150M francs (reparations for "lost property" = people)
  Haiti paid this until 1947 — crippled development for 143 years
  (NY Times investigation, 2022: confirmed ongoing consequences)

metadata.title: Sugar Crops - Sugarcane, Sugar Beet, and the Sweetness Economy

sections.text:

  Glucose isomerase enzyme (from Streptomyces, Actinoplanes, etc.)
  Glucose ⇌ Fructose (equilibrium reaction, ~50:50 at thermodynamic eq.)
  Process gives ~42% fructose, 53% glucose (HFCS-42)
  Enrichment step (ion exchange) → 90% fructose stream
  Blend HFCS-42 + 90% fructose → HFCS-55 (55% fructose, 45% glucose)

  2. US corn subsidies → corn very cheap
  3. HFCS is liquid (easier handling in factories)
  4. HFCS cheaper than US sugar by ~30-40%

sections.text: ### The HFCS Health Controversy

metadata.title: Sugar Crops - Sugarcane, Sugar Beet, and the Sweetness Economy

sections.text:
FRUCTOSE METABOLISM (applies to both HFCS and sucrose):
  Glucose: metabolized by all cells; triggers insulin; satiety hormones
  Fructose: metabolized primarily by liver
             Does NOT trigger insulin response
             Does NOT trigger leptin (satiety hormone) response
             Excess → de novo lipogenesis (liver fat synthesis)
             → VLDL, triglycerides, HDL changes
             High fructose intake associated with:
               Metabolic syndrome, NAFLD (non-alcoholic fatty liver)
               Hypertension (uric acid from fructose metabolism)

metadata.title: Sugar Crops - Sugarcane, Sugar Beet, and the Sweetness Economy

sections.text:
CLAIM: HFCS is uniquely harmful → NOT WELL-SUPPORTED
  The harm is from excess fructose (from any source)
  At equal doses, HFCS and sucrose produce similar metabolic effects
  The correlation of HFCS introduction (1975) with obesity rise:
    Confounded by total caloric increase + ultra-processed food rise
    Cannot isolate HFCS as independent variable from correlation data
```

sections.text:
| Sugar-System Question | Use This Frame | Watch-Out |
|---|---|---|
| Why did sugar become a geopolitical commodity? | Tropical cane + immediate processing + plantation scale | Cheap sweetness was built on coerced labor and trade protection, not just agronomy |
| Cane or beet? | Same refined sucrose, different climate and political economy | "Cane sugar" branding is mostly marketing after refining |
| Why did beet sugar matter strategically? | Temperate substitute for colonial cane | Napoleon's blockade proved supply security could drive crop adoption |
| Why did HFCS win in the US? | Corn wet milling plus sugar tariffs/quotas and liquid handling | The advantage is policy/logistics as much as chemistry |
| Is HFCS uniquely harmful? | Compare fructose dose from HFCS and sucrose | Excess sweetener intake is the issue; HFCS correlation is not causation |
| What does molasses indicate? | Refining stage and residual mineral/flavor load | Blackstrap is a byproduct, not a health counterweight to sugar |
| What should a supply-chain reader track? | Labor regime, land use, water, tariffs, coproducts | Sweetness systems externalize costs differently by crop and region |

sections.text: **"Raw sugar" ≠ unrefined.** Raw sugar (turbinado, demerara, muscovado) is partially refined — it has some molasses remaining. It is not nutritionally superior to white sugar in any meaningful way for the quantities typically consumed.

metadata.title: Sugar Crops - Sugarcane, Sugar Beet, and the Sweetness Economy

sections.text: **Honey ≠ significantly different from sugar metabolically.** Honey is ~40% fructose + 35% glucose (similar to invert sugar/HFCS). The antimicrobial and antioxidant properties are real but require therapeutic doses, not food doses. As a sweetener: similar to sugar.

metadata.title: Sugar Crops - Sugarcane, Sugar Beet, and the Sweetness Economy

sections.text: **Agave syrup is high in fructose.** "Natural" agave nectar: ~56-90% fructose depending on brand/processing. Higher fructose content than HFCS-55. The "low glycemic index" is because fructose doesn't raise blood glucose — but it still stresses liver metabolism.

metadata.title: Sugar Crops - Sugarcane, Sugar Beet, and the Sweetness Economy

sections.text: **Sugar is not "addictive" in the clinical sense.** Animal studies show binge-eating of sugar can show addiction-like behaviors (dopamine release, tolerance). In human studies, the evidence for sugar addiction is weaker — compulsive sugar-eating is often driven by dietary restriction and food environment, not neurochemical dependency equivalent to drug addiction.

metadata.title: Stimulant Crops - Coffee, Tea, and Cacao

sections.text: The three great stimulant crops — coffee, tea, and cacao — share one important characteristic: they were all considered luxury goods or medicines before they became everyday commodities, and all three changed the intellectual and social life of the civilizations that adopted them. Coffee houses preceded the Enlightenment. Tea became a geopolitical flashpoint. Cacao was sacred currency.

L-THEANINE IN TEA
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
L-theanine (an amino acid unique to Camellia sinensis):
  Crosses blood-brain barrier
  Promotes alpha brain wave activity (relaxed alertness)
  GABA-ergic: mild anxiolytic effect
  Increases dopamine and serotonin

metadata.title: Stimulant Crops - Coffee, Tea, and Cacao

Caffeine + L-theanine combination (tea):
  "Mindful alertness" vs pure caffeine (coffee) "jangly" stimulation
  L-theanine reduces caffeine-induced anxiety/jitteriness
  Synergistic on attention, reaction time
  Ratio in brewed tea: ~2:1 L-theanine to caffeine

CACAO BOTANY AND FLAVOR DEVELOPMENT
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
TREE BIOLOGY:
  Cauliflory: flowers + pods grow directly on trunk/large branches
              (not on young shoots like most fruit)
  Requires specific midges (Forcipomyia) for pollination
  Very low pollination success: ~1% of flowers → fruit
  Pod: 500g, contains 30-50 seeds ("beans") in white pulp

metadata.title: Stimulant Crops - Coffee, Tea, and Cacao

sections.text:
CACAO TYPES:
  Criollo: original Mesoamerican, delicate, low yield, high flavor
  Forastero: West African bulk production (75-80% of world supply)
  Trinitario: hybrid; intermediate quality/yield

metadata.title: Stimulant Crops - Coffee, Tea, and Cacao

sections.text:
FERMENTATION AND DRYING (critical for chocolate flavor):
  Pods opened → seeds + pulp in fermentation box/heap
  Duration: 3-7 days (Forastero shorter, Criollo longer)
  Yeast (day 1-2): sugars → ethanol; temperature rises to 50°C
  Bacteria (day 2-7): ethanol → acetic acid; kills embryo; pH drops

metadata.title: Stimulant Crops - Coffee, Tea, and Cacao

sections.text:
CONCHING (Rodolphe Lindt, 1879):
  Grinding + kneading for 12-72+ hours
  Long conching: reduces acidity, particle size (20μm → <20μm = smooth)
  Develops flavor, removes volatiles
  Creates smooth chocolate mouthfeel (lecithin also helps)
  Lindt's original discovery: left machine running overnight by accident
    → next day: remarkably smooth chocolate
    → invented the "fondant" style
```

sections.text: **Child labor in West African cacao — the modern supply chain problem:** The parallel to the sugar/slavery history in 07-SUGAR-CROPS.md is direct and ongoing. Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana together produce ~65% of global cacao. Tulane University/NORC longitudinal studies (2019-2021) found ~1.56 million child laborers in cacao farming in those two countries — children performing hazardous work (machete use, chemical pesticide exposure, heavy loads). The 2001 Harkin-Engel Protocol committed the chocolate industry to eliminating "worst forms" of child labor by 2005, then revised to 2010, then 2020 — all missed. The structural cause: cacao farmer household income averages $0.78–$1.29/day in Côte d'Ivoire (below the extreme poverty line), family farming requires all household labor, and the commodity price structure does not create surplus for hiring adult workers. Certification schemes (Fair Trade, Rainforest Alliance) cover ~14-20% of cacao supply. The certification premium rarely reaches farming households fully. This is structurally identical to the sugar economics that drove plantation slavery: a low-margin commodity where cost pressure flows entirely to the labor base.

CHOCOLATE CRYSTAL POLYMORPHISM (tempering)
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Cocoa butter can form 6 crystal forms (polymorphs I-VI)
  Form V (β₂): the desired form
  Melts at 34°C (mouth temperature) → snap when cold, melts in hand
  Shiny surface, good flavor release

metadata.title: Stimulant Crops - Coffee, Tea, and Cacao

sections.text:
If untempered: Form IV crystals form on cooling
  Bloom: white streaks/patches = wrong crystal polymorph (fat bloom)
         OR moisture: sugar bloom (white, grainy)
  Soft texture, no snap, dull surface

metadata.title: Stimulant Crops - Coffee, Tea, and Cacao

sections.text:
TEMPERING PROCESS:
  Melt chocolate (~50°C) — all crystals melt
  Cool to ~27°C: Form IV + V crystals seed
  Reheat to ~31-32°C: melts Form IV, leaves only Form V seed crystals
  Cool: Form V seeds nucleate uniform crystallization

metadata.title: Stimulant Crops - Coffee, Tea, and Cacao

sections.text:
CHOCOLATE TYPES:
  Dark: cocoa solids + cocoa butter + sugar (no milk)
  Milk: + milk solids (~14-25%); lower cacao, creamier, lower melting point
  White: cocoa butter + milk + sugar, NO cocoa solids
         Not "chocolate" by strict definition (no cocoa mass)
  Ruby: 4th type (2017, Barry Callebaut): naturally pink, fruity flavor
        Special processing of specific Forastero beans; pH + temperature
```

| Crop / Commodity Question | Use This Frame | Watch-Out |
|---|---|---|
| Why did coffeehouses matter socially? | Cheap stimulant plus public discussion infrastructure | The institution mattered as much as the beverage |
| Arabica or robusta? | Altitude/flavor/disease-resistance tradeoff | "Better" depends on product: specialty cup, espresso body, instant coffee, or climate resilience |
| Why does processing dominate coffee flavor? | Natural, washed, and honey processes change fermentation and defect risk | Terroir is filtered through processing control |
| Why does green tea differ from black tea? | Enzyme deactivation vs full oxidation | "Fermentation" is often used loosely; most tea color is oxidation, not microbial fermentation |
| Why does tea feel different from coffee? | Caffeine plus L-theanine and slower consumption pattern | It still contains caffeine; calm alertness is not absence of stimulant load |
| Why does cacao need fermentation? | Microbial fermentation kills embryo and creates flavor precursors | Roasting cannot fully rescue unfermented beans |
| Why does chocolate require tempering? | Cocoa-butter polymorph control | Form V gives snap/sheen; wrong crystals cause bloom |
| What makes the stimulant-crop supply chain ethically loaded? | Plantation labor, colonial trade, poverty-price squeeze | Taste culture often hides coercive commodity history |

sections.text: **Cacao ≠ cocoa.** Cacao = the plant and unprocessed beans. Cocoa = the processed powder (Dutch process or natural). "Cacao powder" marketing = raw unroasted product (or marketing). "Cocoa powder" = roasted. Functionally similar; flavor slightly different.

sections.text: **Dark chocolate isn't "health food."** Epidemiological associations with flavonoid content are real but confounded. A 30g piece of 70% dark chocolate has ~170 calories and ~10g saturated fat. The flavonoid dose that shows cardiovascular benefit in research is typically 200-400mg/day — achievable from dark chocolate but also from tea, berries, or wine.

sections.text: **Caffeine does not "give" you energy.** It blocks adenosine receptors that signal tiredness. Your actual energy state is unchanged. The underlying sleep debt accumulates regardless of caffeine intake.

sections.text: **White chocolate is not a fraud — just a different product.** Cocoa butter is the extracted fat from the cacao bean. White chocolate uses it along with milk and sugar. No cocoa solids = no characteristic chocolate flavor/color. Still a cacao product; just the most processed fraction.
